entry.title: Human Oversight Is Not Enough: Reflections from HCOMP 2026 on the Risks of AI-Assisted Decision-Making

link.title: Human Oversight Is Not Enough: Reflections from HCOMP 2026 on the Risks of AI-Assisted Decision-Making

entry.content:
By Bing Tuo

Ultimately, the partnership between humans and AI could end up being more dangerous than AI acting on its own. The idea of keeping a “human in the loop” for high-stakes decisions involving AI may seem comforting, but it assumes that the human in question is actually capable of providing meaningful oversight. The question, therefore, should not only be: “Is there a human in the loop?” but also: “Is that human cognitively equipped to provide meaningful oversight?” This question stayed with me throughout HCOMP 2026 and increasingly shaped how I thought about AI safety, human–AI collaboration, and my own research.

The ACM Conference on Human-AI Complementarity and Alignment (HCOMP) is a premier venue for sharing the latest research on human–AI complementarity and alignment. The HCOMP community studies and designs systems that bring together the complementary strengths of human and artificial intelligence to achieve outcomes that neither could accomplish alone, while ensuring that such collaboration is ethical, safe, and intentional.

This year, the conference took place in Washington, DC, from September 27–30. Our paper, “Easy to Read, Easy to Trust: How Processing Fluency in LLM Explanations Drives Over-Reliance in Hate Speech Moderation,” received a Best Paper Honorable Mention Award, and I was grateful for the opportunity to present our collaborative work and findings to such a welcoming and engaging audience.

This was my first accepted conference paper, so almost every aspect of the experience felt new and refreshing. With curiosity and excitement, I set out on my own little “Journey to the West.”

The Event

From academia and industry to government, Artificial Intelligence (or Superintelligence) Safety is becoming an increasingly important topic. An overarching consensus among scholars, practitioners, and policymakers is that, no matter how powerful superintelligence becomes, its decision-making processes need to remain understandable to humans, and human agency must always be preserved.

However, as the capabilities of superintelligence advance rapidly, our ability to understand and critically engage with these systems is increasingly falling behind. In his keynote on Collaborative Futures with Intelligent Machines, Eric Horvitz, Chief Scientific Officer at Microsoft, emphasised that the goal should not simply be to develop more capable AI, but to ensure that increasingly capable systems remain intelligible, accountable, and aligned with human aims. More concerningly, he warned that the window for achieving such a future may be narrowing. Without sustained efforts to preserve intelligibility and meaningful human oversight, we risk becoming increasingly dependent on systems that we can neither adequately understand nor effectively guide—fundamentally changing the relationship between people and the intelligent systems they create.

This concern reminded me of a recent news report that illustrates the limits of simply keeping a human “in the loop.” CNN reported on 18 September that, amid the war with Iran, the US military had been preparing to board a Chinese vessel in the Middle East that was believed to be transporting components associated with a nuclear weapons programme. According to the report, this assessment originated from an intelligence analyst using AI, which had misidentified the ship’s cargo and produced what sources described as an “entirely false” intelligence report. Military aircraft were reportedly already in the air before the error was discovered, with one source suggesting that the incident came dangerously close to triggering a confrontation between two nuclear-armed powers.

What struck me about this case is that it represents a very different form of AI-enabled existential risk from the scenarios that often dominate discussions of superintelligence. The immediate danger did not arise from an autonomous superintelligent system independently deciding to take an action against human interests. Rather, it emerged from a hybrid human–AI decision-making system: AI generated or shaped the intelligence, humans interpreted and trusted that intelligence, and humans remained responsible for the consequential decision. The risk, therefore, is not only that future AI systems may become too powerful for humans to control. It is also that humans may increasingly make high-stakes decisions through AI-mediated information environments that subtly shape what they perceive, believe, and ultimately decide.

How can we protect humans from potential cognitive vulnerabilities within hybrid human–AI teams, enabling more resilient decision-making and a genuine decision advantage?

In search of answers, I joined a workshop titled Cognitive Security (CogSec) for Human–AI Systems organised by a group of Stanford researchers. CogSec frames cognitive security—the integrity of the conditions under which individuals and groups can reason for themselves—as an emerging research agenda. The workshop was anchored by a hands-on session focused on developing the Cognitive Vulnerability and Mitigation Catalog (CVMC). The CVMC provides a structured schema that connects AI affordances with associated cognitive vulnerabilities and pairs them with candidate mitigations, evaluation metrics, burden-and-equity considerations, and governance mechanisms. Through this framework, the workshop sought not only to identify how AI might shape or compromise human reasoning, but also to develop systematic approaches for preserving human agency and strengthening decision resilience in increasingly capable human–AI systems.

My first impression of the workshop was the remarkable diversity of the participants’ backgrounds. The room brought together frontline lawyers and doctors, educators, government officials, intelligence professionals, social scientists, psychologists, military personnel, representatives from philanthropic organisations, and even an engineer involved in designing an AI-assisted warfare decision-making system for Australia’s future nuclear-powered submarine programme. This diversity gave me a rare opportunity to examine my own research from perspectives far beyond my usual disciplinary context. It was also deeply encouraging: across these very different domains, I could genuinely feel the importance and practical relevance of the questions my work is trying to address.

At the same time, much of the discussion remained focused on identifying and characterising potential risks within human–AI teams, rather than on established approaches for mitigating them. To me, this reflects how early the field of cognitive security still is. As AI becomes embedded in increasingly consequential decision-making processes, there is an urgent need to move beyond identifying generic risks towards understanding the specific cognitive vulnerabilities that emerge in different AI-assisted decision-making scenarios—and, importantly, developing and evaluating interventions that can mitigate them.

One of my biggest questions after the workshop is: How should we evaluate human–AI collaboration? Or, more fundamentally, what do we actually expect human–AI collaboration to achieve, especially when AI outperforms humans?

This leads me to think about how the human–AI relationship may transition as AI evolves.

My previous experience working with the content moderation team at TikTok gave me a direct view of the roles & responsibility transition between human and AI. Initially, human moderators worked alongside AI systems to make moderation decisions, while their decisions also generated labelled data that could be used to further improve the AI. As the system became sufficiently capable, parts of the work previously undertaken by humans could increasingly be automated. In this model, human–AI collaboration can therefore be transitional rather than an enduring end state: humans help improve the system until the system becomes capable of replacing some of the human work.

If task performance or accuracy remains our primary evaluation metric, there is an uncomfortable logical endpoint. We can continue training AI with more data until, for a particular task, it becomes more capable, consistent, and cost-efficient than humans. Once AI reliably outperforms humans according to the metric we have chosen, there is little performance-based justification for keeping humans in the loop.

Research on human–human collective intelligence also suggests that complementarity does not arise automatically from collaboration. In many settings, collaboration is most valuable when team members contribute differentiated but sufficiently complementary capabilities; when capability asymmetries become too large, interaction can instead constrain the stronger performer. If this insight can be extended to human–AI collaboration, it means that human–AI interaction & collaboration is most valuable only when humans and AI possess comparable and complementary capabilities.

Luckily, for many specialised tasks, of course, such endpoint has not yet been reached. Training data may remain scarce or imperfect, and AI may still lack the contextual knowledge required to dominate the task. More importantly, in high-stakes domains, humans may need to remain involved for reasons that extend beyond predictive performance—including accountability, legitimacy, ethical judgement, contestability, and the preservation of human agency.

These should be our main battlefields of our research.

The question, then, is not simply whether a human–AI team outperforms humans or AI alone, but whether the collaboration preserves humans’ capacity to reason independently, recognise AI errors, intervene effectively, and remain meaningfully responsible for decisions. Accuracy, therefore, cannot be the sole optimisation target. A system may improve task performance while eroding human judgement—the ability to question recommendations, detect failures, and make independent decisions. From a cognitive-security perspective, preserving these capabilities matters even when overall performance improves.

In the main session, I presented our latest work on how the processing fluency of AI explanations can increase human trust and reliance on AI, and explained the underlying cognitive mechanism through the lens of the meta-reasoning framework. When we reason, we are constantly making a second-order decision: should I keep thinking, or is what I have seen good enough? This decision is not determined solely by actual accuracy. Instead, we rely on heuristic cues such as processing fluency—how easy information feels to understand. Fluent information can generate a “feeling of rightness” (FOR), which signals to our slower, analytical reasoning system that further scrutiny may not be necessary. The problem is that fluency is a fallible cue: something can feel right because of how it is presented, rather than because it is actually correct.

Our findings make this distinction particularly important. Participants spent nearly twice as long processing natural-language rationales, meaning that they were not simply skimming or ignoring the explanations. Yet they perceived these rationales as less effortful and more satisfying, and the rationales produced the largest increase in confidence. Objectively, however, there was no corresponding improvement in decision accuracy. In other words, the natural-language explanations were absorbed, but not sufficiently interrogated. This suggests that over-reliance was not caused by a failure of attention. Rather, people paid attention, but the fluency of the explanation provided a metacognitive signal that effectively told them: “this makes sense; you can stop checking now.”

The finding that different forms of AI explanation can influence human–AI team decisions is not, by itself, new. What our study highlights is the limitation of examining only their surface-level effects on team performance. Aggregate measures such as accuracy, trust, or reliance can conceal important differences in how people actually process and respond to AI-generated information. More importantly, without examining the underlying cognitive mechanisms, we cannot explain why particular explanations produce over-reliance. And without understanding that “why,” it becomes difficult to design targeted interventions that mitigate these emerging cognitive vulnerabilities while preserving the benefits of AI assistance.

To sum up, in the context of rapid advances in AI, a human-centred principle is becoming increasingly important for AI and HCI research. AI should actively behave in ways aligned with human values, adapted to human capabilities, and supportive of human agency, rather than forcing humans to understand how AI works or communicate in the language of AI. After all, it is humans who will ultimately use and live with AI. Following this perspective, several new questions have caught my attention, and I am particularly interested in discussing and exploring them in the future:

  1. What happens when the capability gap between humans and AI becomes too large? In the near future, if AI—or even superintelligence (SI)—outperforms humans on almost every task with objectively assessable answers, and the knowledge asymmetry between humans and AI becomes too great for humans to meaningfully catch up, will the relationship between humans and AI begin to flip? If so, how should we redesign our current interfaces and dialogue frameworks to accommodate this shift? It may become increasingly strange to expect a far more capable AI to simply follow poorly formulated human prompts. Instead, AI could become more proactive in everyday life—not merely responding to instructions, but offering guidance, identifying problems, and even asking humans to take particular actions. This raises a fundamental question: what should “human-centred” AI mean when the human is no longer the most capable agent in the collaboration?
  2. What should a human–AI system optimise for beyond performance? If some of the most consequential risks arise not only from how AI behaves, but also from how humans behave when working with AI, then performance complementarity alone may be an insufficient goal. The next generation of human–AI collaboration may need to be evaluated not only by whether the team produces better outcomes, but also by whether human judgement remains resilient throughout the process. Particularly under borderline, ambiguous, or uncertain conditions, we may need to pay greater attention to collective sensemaking: whether humans and AI can jointly develop, challenge, and revise their understanding of a situation rather than simply converge on an answer.
  3. What can human–human collaboration teach us about human–AI collaboration? Many of the challenges now emerging in human–AI teams—trust, authority, expertise asymmetry, disagreement, coordination, and over-reliance—are not entirely new. Decades of research on human teams may already offer important lessons about why collaboration succeeds or fails. The question is whether, and under what conditions, these lessons can be transferred to human–AI collaboration. As we move from model-centred AI towards human-centred AI, the key may therefore be to understand what makes AI fundamentally different from a human collaborator—its capabilities, limitations, communication patterns, authority, and perceived intelligence—and then determine how established principles of collaboration should be adapted accordingly.

Four days at the conference left me with many great memories. Here are a few I’d like to share, especially with those who are new to academic conferences.

Talking to people. My favourite part of the conference was actually the poster session—not only because we had a great session host, but because it gave us the opportunity to interact with people and exchange ideas in real time. The journey of doing research can often feel lonely, and the positive feedback loop is usually very long. Having friends who share similar interests and can relate to what you are going through makes the journey much more enjoyable. Talking with them not only encouraged me, but also sparked many new ideas. I was a little shy at the beginning, but after starting a few conversations, I quickly realised how awesome and supportive everyone was. I truly believe that some of the people I met there will become lifelong friends.

Experiencing the city. Although the jet lag completely messed up my sleep routine, it gave me the chance to get up early on the last day of the conference and go for an 8 km run around the National Mall. To my surprise, Washington, DC reminded me quite a lot of my hometown, Beijing—the monumental architecture, expansive parks, broad streets, and mature trees all felt strangely familiar. Walking through Arlington National Cemetery and watching the guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier also gave me a profound sense of peace. It reminded me that one thing great countries can share is a deep respect for those who sacrificed their lives in war and an enduring commitment to remembering them.

On a lighter note, I was almost hit by an acorn thrown down by a squirrel. I wanted to keep it as a souvenir—too bad I couldn’t bring it back to Australia!
entry.summary: Asking “Is there a human in the loop?” is not enough — we also need to ask whether that human is cognitively equipped to provide meaningful oversight.

entry.title: Designing the oversight hotzenplotz: as we become humans in the loop, what becomes of our work?

link.title: Designing the oversight hotzenplotz: as we become humans in the loop, what becomes of our work?

entry.content:
Designing the Oversight Hotzenplotz: What Should AI Leave for Us Humans to Do?

In our latest reading group, we discussed Klapperich and Hassenzahl’s wonderfully strange paper “Hotzenplotz – Reconciling Automation with Experience”, along with a follow-up-ish study on automated driving “Driving Hotzenplotz: A Hybrid Interface for Vehicle Control Aiming to Maximize Pleasure in Highway Driving”. For context to the readers, the original Hotzenplotz is an electric coffee grinder with a functionally unnecessary manual crank added to “create meaning”. The paper asks a deceptively simple question: when automation makes something easier, faster, or more efficient, what human experience might it remove? The authors describe this as a kind of “experiential amputation”: automation can save labour, but it may also remove agency, skill, involvement, judgement, meaning, ritual or pleasure (e.g., manually grinding coffee beans).

As a group, we found the paper playful, slightly odd, and methodologically imperfect. The language is sometimes silly, the study is small, the statistics are not very detailed, and the work clearly comes from a pre-modern AI time. But we used it as a provocation to discuss a question that is becoming increasingly urgent in human-centred AI: when AI automates (part of) a decision task, what kind of human work should be preserved, and why?

From catching errors to preserving meaningful work

A lot of work on human oversight of AI focuses on whether humans can detect and correct AI errors. That is certainly important. But our discussion kept returning to the design of work that is human oversight of AI. How do we deliberately plan and design oversight work such that while it supports the human in detecting and correcting errors, it also preserves meaning and willingness to do the work? What meaningful parts of human work might be amputated in oversight roles, and is there a Hotzenplotz design move here?

We used a worksheet activity to think through this. Lab members picked a domain of their choosing, which included radiology, peer review, research work, coding agents, and content moderation. For each domain, we went around the table and discussed aspects such as what does the AI automate, what human contribution might be “amputated”, and what would a meaningful oversight design preserve. We arrived on several interesting bits of discussion.

First, automation often removes not just effort, but also expert judgement. In radiology, for e.g., AI might automate detection, measurement, or even report generation. But the meaningful human contribution may lie in deciding what is worth highlighting, interpreting findings in a clinical context, and writing reports that are useful to other clinicians. This goes beyond information processing to finding pleasure and taking pride in exercising professional judgement.

Second, automation can threaten learning and skill maintenance. This came up strongly in our discussions of coding agents and research assistants. AI tools can make people more ambitious because they lower the barrier to trying things. Think of how many months it used to take to build a web-based research prototype five years ago, from an idea to a deployment-ready prototype, and then think about how people can replicate that within weeks today, if not days! No doubt AI tools are making us efficient, but as a byproduct, they are also reducing our need to struggle through hard parts of the work, and that struggle is often where learning happens. One of the lab members framed the ideal AI research assistant not as a tool that produces the answer but as one whose job is to improve the human researcher’s skills and abilities.

Third, we discussed how meaningful work is often social. Peer review was a good example. An AI could summarise a paper or collate reviews, but reviewing is also a form of community participation. It involves implicit judgements, venue/journal norms that often cannot be/haven’t been formalised, and most importantly, a sense of service to the research community. If review becomes fully automated, we might lose part of the scholarly community that the process helps maintain. The group also raised a similar point for content moderation. Some cases with clearly harmful content may be appropriate to automate. But many moderation decisions are about (implicit, experience-driven) community norms: what kind of space is this, what counts as acceptable here, etc. In such cases, moderation is not just an act of removing content but part of community governance and maintenance. Fully automating it likely takes something of value away from the human moderators of these communities.

A decorative Hotzenplotz crank?

A recurring concern was that “meaningful human involvement” can easily become fake agency. The Hotzenplotz crank is quite charming in a coffee grinder. But during AI oversight, an analogous decorative crank could introduce new risks. The human might be asked to approve, sign off, or “stay in the loop” without having the time, information, authority, or organisational support needed to make a judgement.

Work, labour, and the right level of automation

One of the most useful distinctions that emerged was between work and labour. Labour is the repetitive, tedious, annoying, low-value part of a task. Work is the part that carries judgement, craft, care, etc.

Of course, the distinction is not fixed. Grinding coffee may be a meaningful ritual for one person and an annoying laborious task for another. Writing a peer review may be community service for one person and a burden for another. The same task can have a different meaning depending on context. We argued that this context-dependence/context-sensitive design is crucial for AI oversight. Several examples pointed towards a middle ground. In peer review, AI might support note-taking, collation, or summarisation, while preserving reading, judgement, and final evaluation for the human. In radiology, AI might support writing clinical reports, while preserving interpretation, judgement, and diagnosis for the human. In content moderation, AI might remove clear cut harmful content, while humans can deliberate over more community-specific.

Future directions for human-centred AI oversight

The discussion left us with several open questions for future research.

First, we agreed that we need to better understand the psychological needs of oversight. The automated driving paper asks which psychological needs need to be fulfilled for driving to remain pleasurable. For AI oversight, the equivalent question might be: which psychological needs need to be fulfilled for oversight to remain meaningful, sustainable, and effective? Autonomy, competence, professional pride, learning, social connection, responsibility, and purpose all seemed important in our discussion.

Second, we need to think beyond interfaces and towards work design. Meaningful oversight requires rethinking the very nature of human-AI collaboration itself. We also need to focus on preserving the skills and motivation of the overseer. If AI helps people produce faster work while gradually eroding their ability to perform the task, then the system may be efficient in the short term but harmful in the long term.

The Hotzenplotz papers do not offer a direct model for AI oversight, but they do help sharpen the questions we should be asking. Human oversight is not simply a matter of placing a person after an AI system to approve, correct, or contest its outputs. It changes the nature of the human role: from doing the original task to judging the work of an automated system, from producing decisions to evaluating them. That shift has consequences for expertise, agency, accountability, and the very meaning of work. For human-centred AI, the challenge is therefore not only to design better oversight interfaces, but to design better oversight work: work that gives people the information and intervention mechanisms needed to exercise judgement meaningfully.

Watch this space for how we go about tackling this grand challenge.

entry.title: Geoguessr: A new scientific frontier
entry.content:
Geoguessr: A new scientific frontier

Ever played Geoguessr? The globally recognised (and rewarded) online game in which you have to guess where you are in the world when landed in a random Google street view location? If you haven’t you should because it’s weirdly fun (and challenging unless you happen to be a geography nerd!).

But you should also play it because it might just provide us scientists with interesting insights into how people make decisions in naturalistic settings (I agree that Geoguessr is not exactly “naturalistic” but it’s probably more so than a university lab, and at least these decision-makers are intrinsically motivated!).

The really lucky thing for us, however, is that Geoguessr players like to make videos of themselves at work. In so doing, they are effectively providing us with hours and hours of data.

…looks like uh, it’s going to be Chile. It’s a big city here. It’s coastal, for sure. It’s very flat. Hard to see how green it is. Do we see any hills? That would be like the big thing to check here, I think. So, that doesn’t say the city on it. I don’t think it has an area code, but I don’t know area codes in uh, Chile.

This is very interesting because it gives us concurrent decision-making think-aloud data, sourced from a range of expertise (novices to pros), and with associated outcomes such as whether they got the decision right.

And what’s more interesting is that when listening to the real pro players (the ones who win thousands of dollars) you see them intuitively balancing their quick-fire expertise with a slower and more deliberative style of thinking. And this is exactly what is being debated right now in the scholarly world of decision-making research. Is intuitive thinking (AKA fast, unconscious, automatic, emotional, System 1) separate from deliberative (AKA slow, rational, conscious, logical, System 2)? Is deliberative thinking superior to intuitive? Is intuitive more likely to be biased? And what’s really interesting (to me at least!) — how, why, and when do you switch between the two modes of thinking?

Digging into this area of research, I’ve come across the intriguing concept of paradox theory. This construct comes from the organizational, management, and leadership literature, and is often related to what’s referred to as strategic decision-making (which implies complex and high risk). The paradox describes a tension between intuitive and deliberative thinking styles and would be evident when a decision-maker becomes aware that two (or more) potential decision outcomes are misaligned. It is in being both aware of and responding to this misalignment that the decision-maker can leverage better decision outcomes.

“…probably going to be Indonesia. Tons of coconut palms here, to our northwest. Like a West Java kind of vibe there for maybe. It’s very flat though. Okay, so I want to check out South. Can we see mountains? Not really. Kind of suspicious. What about the architecture? Definitely looks like Javanese architecture, but it’d be up here, I guess.”

So far the evidence in this space is sparse and only qualitative and for this reason, calls have been made for empirical evidence to support new models of decision-making. Lucky for us, Geoguessrs may lead us to just such evidence — providing us as it does with hundreds of narrated, complex, uncertain, and time-constrained decision challenges. All we have to do is analyse each decision using an adapted form of content analysis in order to quantify how many indicators of paradoxical cognitive there are (or are not).

So, watch this space as we become more familiar with the hectic worlds of Geoguessr pros like Radu, Blinky, Rainbolt and Zi8zag.

entry.title: Farewell and Best Wishes to ASCI lab member Chengbo Zheng

link.title: Farewell and Best Wishes to ASCI lab member Chengbo Zheng

entry.content:
The ASCI lab recently got together for a farewell dinner to celebrate Chengbo, who is now heading to the Max Planck Institute in Freiburg, Germany, to continue his research journey. While we’ll certainly miss having him around the lab, we’re excited for this next chapter in his research career!

Thank you for being such a wonderful part of the team, Chengbo! Wishing you all the best in Freiburg, and we look forward to hearing about all the exciting work ahead.

entry.title: ARC Centre of Excellence success in ASCI

link.title: ARC Centre of Excellence success in ASCI

entry.content:
Tim is one of 17 chief investigators part of a new $94.6 million ARC Centre of Excellence to empower workers in the digital age.

The ARC Centre of Excellence for Quality Work in a Digital Age (QWiDA) will work with international researchers, industry, and government on how workers and organisations can better use technology in the workplace. Tim will lead the UQ node, which will investigate augmenting working with artificial intelligence and automation, looking at effects beyond just technology efficiency, such as the effect on work quality, worker well-being, and investigating important topics such as skill erosion from artificial intelligence.

Tim is joined at UQ by Prof Andrew Neal and A/Prof Tim Ballard, both from the School of Psychology. Other nodes will operate from Curtin University, The University of Melbourne, Adelaide University, UNSW, Swinburne University of Technology, and QUT.

You can read more about it at the QWiDA webpage
entry.summary: Tim is one of 17 chief investigators part of a new $94.6 million ARC Centre of Excellence to empower workers in the digital age.

entry.title: ASCA success at ASCI!
entry.content:
Tim was fortunate to be awarded $2.8 million dollars for a new project Scalable Human Augmentation with Deference and Explainability, awarded by the Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator (ASCA). SHADE is one of handful of projects announced as part of ASCA’s Decision Advantage program.

Tim will lead the project, with CIs A/Prof Pier Howe from the University of Melbourne, and Dr Leon Clark from Lockheed Martin Australia.

The project will investigate how to make decisions at scale, experimenting with techniques such as ‘learning to defer’, and aiming to pioneer new project in the area of ‘explainability sets’ – grouping and explaining sets of decisions to reduce cognitive load.

Stay tuned for more once the project beings in February!

entry.title: Humans and AI, what (and how) do we think?

link.title: Humans and AI, what (and how) do we think?

entry.content:
Today, many of us are questioning the pros and cons of AI ‘knowledge’ tools. They offer increased efficiencies, but they are also challenging our faith in (and understanding of) information, knowledge, and epistemological accountability. As knowledge workers, we find ourselves sandwiched awkwardly between the experience (and promise) of AI-provisioned comfort and the desire (and need) for human-provisioned growth. Navigating this emerging paradigm shift — in which our knowledge practices, productions, and consumptions are being re-invented before our very eyes — leaves many of us struggling to find the right balance of industry push, AI delegation, and individual integrity.

So, just how different is this new age of AI-supported thinking (or to put it another way, are we talking calculators or chain reactions)?      

Some scholars are suggesting that, in the light of this latest socio-technical evolution, we must now revise our fundamental understanding of human thought. Where once there was only System 1 and System 2 (gut instinct vs cool intellect), there are now suggestions of a third, described as System 3, or indeed System 0. These ‘third ways’ attempt to describe how humans are now thinking, reasoning, and decision-making with the aid of AI knowledge tools. And, more specifically, how these new integrated modalities have given rise to the need for a new understanding of cognition. The System 3 proponents talk not just of AI-induced human cognitive offloading and overriding, but also of cognitive surrender. This latter state is described as a transfer of control in which humans adopt “AI outputs with minimal scrutiny, and overriding intuition and deliberation”. And often culminating in “adopting the AI’s judgement as their own”. The System 0 proponents describe it slightly less alarmingly as “an artificial, non-biological underlying layer of distributed intelligence that interacts with and augments both intuitive [System 1] and analytical [System 2] thinking”. But they also go on to say this new form of thinking raises important epistemological and ethical concerns, such as dependency, shifting norms, and reduced critical thinking.

These thought provocations would suggest that AI information tools are not just another turn on the technological wheel, but rather represent a fundamental paradigm shift in our knowledge practices. Confronted with this significant re-appraisal of all that we hold dear, context, comparisons, and critiques can be helpful. For instance, it is worth reflecting on the reactions of some when the printing press was invented in the 15th century, the consequences of which were the dissemination of information, stories, and knowledge at a scale never seen before. Leading the charge against the monstrosities of the ‘mechanical movable type printing press’ were the Benedictine monks:

“They shamelessly print, at a negligible price, material which may, alas, inflame impressionable youths, while a true writer dies of hunger. Cure (if you will) the plague which is doing away with the laws of all decency, and curb the printers. They persist in their sick vices, setting Tibullus in type, while a young girl reads Ovid to learn sinfulness. Through printing, tender boys and gentle girls, chaste without foul stain, take in whatever mars purity of mind or body; they encourage wantonness, and swallow up huge gain from it” Fillippo de Strata.

Shifting from monastic mania back to the rigours of science, the System 0 proponents describe AI as an extended form of distributed cognition, the notion of which provides us with a useful structure to help contemplate the question of AI r/evolutions. The notion of distributed cognition has been around for a fair while, and in essence describes thinking that happens not just in an individual’s mind, but that eventuates as a product of thoughts distributed across other people as well as other tools and environments. Examples of distributed cognition range from the humble shopping list compiled collectively via post-its on a fridge door, to the confident GPS system (sometimes) taking us down awkward lanes and unhelpful cul-de-sacs. According to this definition therefore, AI is just another tool that is being harnessed by our well-practiced distributive thinking habits, thereby falling more into the papyrus to printing to predictive algorithms pattern rather than the paradigm shifting need for an entirely new model of human thinking.

But does that really cover it? Is the pervasive integration of a single thinking tool that helps us do anything from managing our diaries, to writing reports, sending emails, coding websites, advising on lifestyle choices (we could go on), is this merely an amped up form of distributed cognition? Or is it, as the third system theorists suggest, doing something more?

The answer is (as ever) yes and no. AI does represent a form of distributed cognition, but no, it’s not as we’ve ever seen it before. And (ironically) in reality AI is actually a somewhat undistributed form of distributed cognition. Because distributed implies a diversity of informational options — across people, objects and place, whereas AI information, although trained on the oh-so-wide world web, has been finely milled, ultra-processed, and artificially reconstituted according to the directives of a handful of extraordinarily well-funded (not to mention geo-politically powerful) technology companies.

And there are other things that also set AI apart from the more established processes of distributed cognition. For instance, the persuasive nature of generative AI’s anthropomorphic conversational interface means that we as humans can’t help but speak to it as we would another human (just think about that uncomfortable feeling of social dissonance brought on when attempting to remove conversational politesse to save on time or tokens!). And we know from both research and headlines, that dialoguing with an AI agent over sustained periods of time produces outcomes similarly associated with human-to-human interpersonal relationships, including emotional investment, reliance, and identity fusion.  

So, to return to the question of calculators or chain reactions, the answer might be better contended with from a more retrospective viewpoint. All technologies have the potential to be disruptive, but their disruptive potential only exists in the minds and (subsequent) actions of their human users. Understanding the potential for AI disruption, whether to military operations, traffic management, or indeed, the foundations of human thought requires (ironically) human thought. And given what we know about the impact of confounds on empirical truth-seeking, ensuring that we investigate the question of human thought before full cognitive surrender, would appear to be wise.
entry.summary: Just how different is thinking with AI - are we talking calculators or chain reactions?

entry.title: Evidence-based scientific thinking and decision-making in everyday life | Dawson et al | 2024

link.title: Evidence-based scientific thinking and decision-making in everyday life | Dawson et al | 2024

entry.content:
This paper takes a rigorous, open-science approach to the question of what factors influence a person’s ability to evaluate information and subsequently make decisions on the basis of that information. The paper is purely dealing with humans reading text, and makes no mention of the source of the information (technology or otherwise). The factors are categorised as ‘individual difference’ variables and ‘perceptual and cognitive behavioural’ variables. The usefulness of the paper lies in it’s up to date synthesis of the literature relating to these factors, and the associated questions these constructs raise when it comes to understanding not only how humans engage with information, but more importantly for our work, how do we want humans to engage with information. Constructs of interest are the two dimensions of epistemic curiosity (these are ‘interest curiosity’ described as “an internally motivated drive to acquire information” and associated with mastery-orientated learning, analytical thinking and enjoyment of problem-solving, and “deprivation curiosity” described as “prompts people to find answers in order to end the uncomfortable state of uncertainty brought on by a knowledge gap”). The ‘intellectual humility’ scale (capturing four factors, for example openness to revising viewpoints), the need for closure scale, the ‘unusual uses’ task (measuring divergent thinking) and the ‘actively open-minded’ scale are all also useful to consider when thinking about the loss of human control that can arise when humans are working with AI decision aids. Key findings were that curiosity, cognitive flexibility, and prosociality were related to engaging with information and discernment of evidence reliability. Also, the perception of social authority (effectively a social dynamic, social identity related concept) was a powerful driver of outcomes, as well as perceived information credibility (even above the actual quality and relevance of the sources).
